The neutral motion asks whether there is sufficient evidence to believe in the resurrection of Jesus. Winger affirms historical evidential sufficiency; Paulogia challenges it and need not establish that no resurrection occurred. Do not strengthen his burden to proving a fully specified natural explanation unless he expressly undertakes that claim.

Winger distinguishes three claimed consensus facts from an additional majority-supported empty tomb. He presents biblical texts as historical evidence without asking the audience to assume inerrancy. His initial facts concern sincere appearance beliefs rather than the truth of a resurrection; preserve the later inference to best explanation, and his distinction between the Twelve as a group title and a literal headcount.

Paulogia grants Jesus existed and died by crucifixion for this debate, accepts Paul believed he saw Jesus, grants early creed dating around five to ten years, and questions evidence for the wider group. Preserve his distinction between reports, sincere experiences and actual bodily resurrection. He explicitly permits miracles in principle (22:37–23:11 and closing); low prior probability is not asserted logical impossibility. Do not adopt Winger’s closing characterization as Paulogia’s actual position.

Paulogia offers mundane possibilities without committing to a complete historical reconstruction; later he asserts Peter/Paul mistakes or deception suffice. Assess what each version actually undertakes. Preserve Winger’s challenges about explanatory fit, group appearances and durability under persecution; distinguish mass hallucination from socially transmitted claims and altered memories.

Paulogia challenges undocumented consensus percentages, gospel independence and eyewitness status, and recantation opportunities. Winger provides claimed textual attestations and historical inferences. Do not import later corrections on screen or independent research to grade these 2018 arguments. Reported percentages, studies, dates, martyrdoms, authorship and interpretations remain speaker claims, not independently verified facts.

Names and references are sometimes misrecognized: Ehrman, Habermas, Licona, Ludemann, Cephas, Acts, Clement, Polycarp, James/Jude/John and Pontius Pilate. Around 33:49 the captions say jesus and baby jude in an acknowledged-name exchange; around 1:03:45–1:04:02 James/Mark/John overlap.
